text: Madam Speaker, last September our government launched a universal breakfast program in all New Brunswick schools. Not some schools. I will say that again: all New Brunswick schools. Close to a year later, we are already seeing concrete results. Every morning, throughout the province, students start their day with a nutritious meal: milk, eggs, bagels, apples, and cheese. Through our partnership with FeedNB, schools are able to offer healthy foods, which are often sourced from our local farms and businesses. For many families, especially with the rising cost of living, this program is making a real difference. It saves parents time and money and reduces stress in their morning routine. And it means students come to class prepared to learn. That is the whole point of it, and I am going to repeat it because it gets lost in the arguing about the cost: students come to class prepared to learn. Every child deserves to start their day on the right foot, Madam Speaker. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in sadness on the passing of Robert Hosford, beloved husband, father, pop pop, uncle, great-uncle, and friend. Robert passed away on Wednesday, November 12, leaving behind a legacy of love, laughter, and adventure. He was a devoted family man. He was the cornerstone of his family — the cornerstone — always putting their needs before his own. I want to say that again, because his family said it to me twice: he put their needs before his own. His love and support knew no bounds, and he was always there to lend a helping hand or offer a listening ear. Robert's warm smile and infectious laugh could light up a room, and his sense of humour could turn even the toughest day into a memorable moment. He was his family's biggest cheerleader, proudly supporting their endeavours and celebrating their success. Whether he was cheering on his favourite team or teaching a lesson, his passion for sports was only matched by his love for his family. Please join me in expressing condolences to Robert's family and friends. Thank you.

Madam Speaker, I want to recognize the outstanding work of Nursing Home Without Walls. Today they are with Horizon Health Network at the Miramichi Regional Hospital, in the main lobby past the gift shop, from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. They are signing seniors up for MyHealthNB. A senior can sit down with someone there, get hands-on help, and reach the point of seeing their own blood work and their own imaging results, securely, on a screen. Bring a Medicare card and an email address. That is the whole list. Horizon staff verify identity and give out the access code right there — no appointment, no registration, nothing booked ahead. Nursing Home Without Walls has been taking barriers down like this in the lives of seniors in our communities for a while now, and seniors stay connected to their own health information, and stay healthy and independent, because of it. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Property owners pay the cost of assessment fee on the property tax bill. That is through Finance and Treasury Board. They also pay charges through their local tax rates, which means the same property owner is paying twice over, once directly on the bill in front of them and once indirectly through the municipal taxes their town or their rural district collects and then hands to Service New Brunswick for assessment services. Both ways. Same person.

Madam Speaker, many New Brunswickers do not know this. They see the visible charge on the tax bill and they assume that is the entirety of the assessment cost. They do not realize the municipality is paying too.

Let me be clear. This motion does not criticize the work performed by Service New Brunswick. Assessment services are necessary. Municipalities require accurate assessments, and Service New Brunswick provides an actual service to municipalities and to rural districts, so nobody here should walk out of this Chamber telling assessors that their work is on trial.

But Finance and Treasury Board is not providing assessment services. It is charging the fee. That is the charge this motion seeks to eliminate, and after years of rising assessments and rising costs, I would argue the time has come to do it.

People feel the government benefits from circumstances they cannot control. No homeowner asked for property values to surge. No senior on a fixed income asked to have a modest house reassessed at a dramatically higher value, and we all know that assessments have gone up in recent years. With COVID-19, and with people moving here from away, home prices went up. Fair market value is a big factor in the assessment process, and that is why the increase was so sharp.

Up go the assessments. Up goes the revenue from this fee. That creates a perception, and the perception is that government does well out of the same increases that keep the rest of them up at night.

Madam Speaker, today is the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, and we recognize the strength, contributions, and resilience of persons with disabilities across New Brunswick. The member for Fredericton South asked in this House last month whether the province intended to "offset" the federal benefit. She used that word, and I want to answer it plainly. This summer we made sure the federal Canada Disability Benefit wouldn't detract from provincial disability programs. No offset. Federal programs are to complement provincial support, not replace it. We remain committed to a province where every person has an equal opportunity to participate fully in our communities, schools, workplaces, and public spaces. Accessibility and inclusion are not optional. They are essential to true equity. Let us keep working together to remove barriers, promote dignity, and ensure that every New Brunswicker can live, work, and thrive without limitations. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Moreover, the treatment of nursing home workers under Premier Higgs' leadership was concerning. I am not a labour lawyer, and I will not pretend I have read every clause of the arbitration changes. I have read enough. This government took nursing home workers to court and suggested that they relocate to Alberta for better wages. I do not know how anyone says that out loud to a woman who has spent 20 years lifting residents out of bed in Bathurst. It was a failure in negotiation and a betrayal of the people who provide essential care to our vulnerable populations. The 16-day school strike, and the emergency orders used to force workers back, raised questions about this government's commitment to meaningful dialogue and to the right to strike. Those measures undermined the very principles of a fair and balanced negotiation process. Watering down binding arbitration, introducing scab-friendly legislation, and this pension bill are a pattern that erodes the foundation of workers' rights. They do not align with the principles of a just and equitable society. It is our duty to scrutinize and question these policies, because the decisions made by government impact the livelihoods of countless individuals and the health of our communities. Madam Deputy Speaker, you will recall the unions expressing their vehement disagreement with the wage-freeze restriction mandate proposed by the Higgs government — the 0% wage mandate in the early years of this government. In the face of a global pandemic, our frontline workers were nothing short of heroes. Their commitment and sacrifices demanded acknowledgement and tangible support. The union leaders rightly asserted that these heroes deserved more than zeroes in their wage agreements.

Madam Speaker, our government has presented the 2026-27 capital budget: $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year, and the largest capital budget ever tabled in this province. Most of that money goes to the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure, for roads, bridges, ferries, and the wharves and culverts nobody thinks about until one of them washes out. The Department of Health will replace medical equipment that is past its life and renovate hospitals. We will build a new school in Shediac and a new school in Moncton, and we will upgrade several other institutions elsewhere in the province. We are doing this because the province underinvested for years and the backlog landed on this generation of students, patients and drivers. These are safety projects and they are quality-of-life projects. Our children will be using these buildings. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, each year, on November 11, we pause to remember the brave men and women who served and continue to serve our country in times of war, conflict, and peacekeeping. Their courage, sacrifice, and unwavering sense of duty have safeguarded the freedom and values we cherish today. We also pay tribute to the families who have carried the burden of separation and grief, and to the veterans who have returned home changed by their service. As we gather at cenotaphs and memorials across New Brunswick, may we renew our commitment to peace, to gratitude, and to never forgetting those who gave everything for Canada. Two minutes. That is what we are asked for. Stand still, and let the wreaths go down. Lest we forget. Lest we forget.

Mr. Speaker, labour relations in this province are strained, and that strain sits over every effort we make together to build prosperity in New Brunswick. This government took a legislative approach and that approach is the reason. We should be talking to workers and their representatives directly, telling them the truth, and keeping our word to them. Workers will trust a government that does those things, and a government that has their trust can weigh what everybody at the table needs.

Mr. Speaker, in December 2019, this Legislature was embroiled in a contentious debate over the essential service legislation, which was specifically focused on the wages of nursing home workers. That bill, Bill 17, imposed conditions on how labour arbitrators could rule on the wages of those workers. It sparked an intense reaction. Members of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions came out against it. They said it would damage their ability to strike and to negotiate a fair wage, and they said it loudly. You could hear how deep the discontent ran.

The law passed. Union leaders decried it as an attack on public-sector labour unions. Sharon Teare, President of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions, avowed that their voice would not be silenced. She said they would keep fighting for better working conditions and keep protecting the rights of nursing home workers, who play a valuable role in our society.

Bill 17 showed how the government and the labour unions in New Brunswick pull against each other on labour rights and on collective bargaining. It showed how hard it is to weigh what a worker needs against what a taxpayer pays and what a finance minister has to answer for.

When we look back at December 2019 and at the passage of Bill 17, we can't forget that there are members sitting in this government now who opposed that bill. They said so out loud. They said they would stand with the labour movement as long as they could. That has changed today.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to recognize the Battle of Vimy Ridge. It was fought on April 9, 1917. It is one of the defining moments in Canada's history. Since 2006, the Vimy Foundation has worked at raising awareness of that battle and educating Canadians about it, and this year's campaign marks the beginning of the lead-up to the 110th anniversary in 2027, which I hope every school in my riding takes part in, because a date on a page does not mean much to a 14-year-old unless somebody in the room makes it mean something. Vimy Week runs from April 2 to 9. Wear the pin. The Vimy Pin is composed of four distinct colours, one for each of the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge, and it stands for their unity and their sacrifice. That is what we are honouring. Their courage. The legacy they left behind, which helped define this nation. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, the member opposite asked earlier what stops this from being abused, so let me answer with the actual text. An employee must have at least 90 days of continuous employment to be eligible for the leave, which aligns with leave provisions in other provinces. The employee is required to inform the employer "as soon as possible" of the need for leave — those are the words in the amendment, and they are not "whenever it suits the employee", as I heard put a few minutes ago. The employer may require reasonable medical documentation confirming that the employee is unable to work due to illness or injury. Those elements support the integrity of the leave and give employers reasonable assurance and predictability. Madam Speaker, this amendment is an important step forward. It strengthens protections for workers at a time when they are most vulnerable while keeping a balance that considers the realities of workplaces across the province, and it supports the objective of New Brunswick remaining a place where people can live and work with dignity. No one should have to choose between their health and their job. This closes a clear gap in the Employment Standards Act. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Our economic development strategy has one priority: build a stronger, more competitive New Brunswick that gives people here somewhere to go. New Brunswick succeeds when our businesses succeed. When a company grows, reaches a new market, and puts money back into its own operation, it hires people, it holds a community together, and it pays into the tax base that funds the services families use every single day. The strategy builds on what we already have. It aims at productivity. It backs the firms that are trying something new, and it helps New Brunswick companies compete in a global economy that will not sit still for them. We are also going after investment and building up the sectors where we can actually win — defence and mining chief among them — and we want that growth to last. Departments will work off the same list of priorities and the same measurable outcomes, and I will be answerable for them. The government cannot do this alone. It takes industry, the universities and colleges, communities, and frankly every member sitting in this House. The people we have shown it to so far like what they see, and what they keep coming back to is that it is clear, it is disciplined, and it says what it will deliver. New Brunswick has what the world wants. We are competing to win, and we are setting the conditions for businesses to grow, for communities to thrive, and for opportunity to spread out past the two or three places that usually get it. A growing economy pays for better services. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I want to recognize the work of Nursing Home Without Walls, which keeps making a real difference for seniors in our communities. Today it is partnering with Horizon Health Network to give seniors hands-on assistance setting up access to MyHealthNB, a secure online portal that lets a person look up their own blood work and their own imaging results rather than waiting on a call back from somebody's office. Staff are there now. They are at the Miramichi Regional Hospital, in the main lobby, today from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. Bring a Medicare card and an email address. That is all it takes to create an account. Horizon staff verify identity and hand over the access code on the spot, and there is no appointment and no registration needed. This is how a barrier comes down. Seniors stay connected to their own health information, and they stay healthy and independent. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, Roméo H. LeBlanc has died at the age of 102. He was an Acadian, and he served in the Second World War. As Minister responsible for Military Affairs, I want to pay tribute to a man who gave this country exceptional service. Mr. LeBlanc did not stop when the war ended. He spent the rest of his life with the veterans' community — visiting them, sitting on committees, chasing down names, photographs, service records, the odd letter home — so that the men and women who served would not be forgotten. He was a courageous man and a dutiful one, and young people who come across his story will be the better for it. On behalf of the government of New Brunswick, I extend my sincerest condolences to his family, to those who loved him, and to the veterans who knew him. We will remember him. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to recognize the enduring significance of the Battle of Vimy Ridge, fought on April 9, 1917, one of the defining moments in Canada's history. Since 2006, the Vimy Foundation has been dedicated to raising awareness and educating Canadians about the battle. This year's campaign marks the beginning of the lead-up to the 110th anniversary of the battle in 2027, a milestone moment in Canada's history. Vimy Week runs from April 2 to 9, and I encourage all members of this House to wear the Vimy Pin. It is composed of four distinct colours, one for each of the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge. By wearing it we honour their courage and their sacrifice and the legacy they left behind. The pin itself is smaller than a dime. Most of them end up in a desk drawer by May. Wear it anyway.

Bill 40 amends the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act, an Act that already tells hospitals how to review a patient safety incident and what to do with what they learn. The government says the amendments will improve how incidents get reviewed, strengthen collaboration, make reviews more consistent, and tell patients and families more. Nobody opposes any of that. But a bill does what it does, not what it means to do.

So what has failed? The Act is on the books already. Are incident reviews not occurring? Are lessons not being shared? Are patients not being informed? Are health authorities ignoring recommendations? Members raised all four at the briefing on the bill, and rightly so. The government has shown us no data pointing to a systemic failure under the current law. Change the law after you find the gap, not before. A doctor diagnoses before treating.

The biggest thing in the bill is a new committee, the New Brunswick Quality of Care and Patient Safety Advisory Committee, which the minister sets up and keeps running. Fine, on paper. Who turns down expert advice on patient safety?

Slow down here. A nurse in Miramichi already answers to Horizon Health Network, a professional regulatory college, an accreditation body, an internal quality review committee, and a patient advocacy office. A nurse an hour west answers to Vitalité Health Network instead. That is five desks before this bill adds a sixth. Are we improving outcomes or adding bureaucracy? Front-line workers keep telling us they fill out forms in the hours they used to spend with patients. Add a reporting layer that improves nothing anyone can measure and you have worsened the very system you set out to help.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Our government's economic development strategy is focused on one priority: building a stronger and more competitive New Brunswick that is a source of opportunity for people in this province. New Brunswick succeeds when our businesses succeed. A company that grows, reaches a new market, or invests in its operations creates jobs, strengthens the community around it, and drives the economic activity that supports the public services families rely on every day.

The strategy builds on our existing strengths. It focuses on productivity, on innovation, and on helping New Brunswick companies compete in a global economy that keeps moving. It reinforces our commitment to attracting investment, to strengthening key sectors such as defence and mining, and to long-term sustainable growth.

We are taking a coordinated and accountable approach that brings departments together around shared priorities and measurable outcomes. This is not work the government can do alone. It takes industry, academia, communities across the province, and the members of this House. Early feedback from stakeholders has been positive, with recognition of our focus on clarity, discipline, and results.

New Brunswick has what the world wants. I was in Sussex two Fridays ago, at a machine shop with eleven employees on the floor. The owner did not ask me about the strategy. He asked whether the apprentice he took on in March would still be here in three years, or gone to Alberta like the last one. That is the file. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in sadness on the passing of Robert Hosford. Robert was a husband, a father, a pop pop, an uncle, a great-uncle, and a friend. He passed away on Wednesday, November 12. What he left behind is love, laughter, and adventure, and I do not think I can improve on that. Robert was a devoted family man. He was the cornerstone of his family and he put their needs before his own, every time. His love and support knew no bounds. He would lend a hand, or he would just listen. His smile and his laugh could light up a room. His sense of humour could turn the toughest day into a memorable one. Anyone who was at the service knows exactly what I mean. He was his family's biggest cheerleader, proud of what they took on and first to celebrate when it went well. Whether he was cheering on his favourite team or teaching a lesson, Robert's passion for sports was matched only by his love for his family. Please join me in expressing condolences to Robert's family and friends. Thank you.

Madam Speaker, Charlie Burrell shows what one person can do. In Little River he has spent his own time and his own energy building a facility and small homes for people who have nowhere to live — people most of us walk past. He saw his friends, and he calls them his friends every single time, homeless on the streets of Moncton, and instead of turning away he did something. He brings them food and clothing. More than that, he treats them like people. He keeps saying that homelessness is not an issue, it is something happening to somebody, and that everyone is owed some kindness and a chance. Others have got involved because he asked them to. Thank you, Charlie. The last time I was out there, he was arguing with a fellow about the price of plywood and losing. The homes have doors that lock. That is the part he wanted me to mention.

Madam Speaker, our government has presented the 2026-27 capital budget, a historic budget of $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year and the largest capital budget ever tabled in our province. The member opposite called it, yesterday, "an election-year road budget." Those were his words, and I would ask him to look at where the money actually goes. Most of the investment is allocated to the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure, to improve our roads, bridges, ferries, and other essential infrastructure. The health care sector will also see significant investment, to modernize our medical equipment and to renovate our hospitals. In education, the capital budget includes building new schools in Shediac and Moncton and upgrading several institutions elsewhere in the province. These investments are essential to deal with the backlog caused by years of underinvestment. When this House resolves itself into the Committee of Supply to open the capital estimates, I invite the member to test every line of it. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I have heard the word "approve" from across the floor a few times this afternoon, and that is the word I want to quarrel with. The bill's aim is to make things easier, not approve them. It is about removing barriers, providing clarity, and ensuring that New Brunswick is prepared to move forward when the time comes. My colleague opposite asked who was at the table. The proposal was drafted in consultation with several departments, including the Office of the Attorney General, Service New Brunswick, the Department of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, and the Department of Indigenous Affairs. The NB Power Board of Directors will continue to oversee all security measures, and that is where financial accountability and risk mitigation sit. The information will be used as the basis of the proposal submitted for government approval, and it will be reviewed before any authorization. Madam Speaker, the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future, and this bill makes sure we meet its challenges with the flexibility and the clarity that will be required. I urge all members of the House to support it and help us take the next step toward securing clean energy for New Brunswickers, today and for decades to come. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, Charlie Burrell is an example of what one person can do in their community. In Little River, he has put his time and his own energy into building a facility and small homes for people experiencing homelessness — people who get overlooked and forgotten. He saw his friends, and that is the word he always uses, homeless on the streets of Moncton, and he stepped up instead of turning away. He gives out food and clothing, and, more than that, he gives people dignity and some hope.

I will be honest with members. I am not an expert on housing policy or on addiction, and I do not know whether what Charlie is doing in Little River can be done anywhere else at any scale. I have asked. I have not got a good answer yet. What I do know is that in February there was a man sleeping in a car behind the Irving, and by March that man had a room with a door on it. Charlie has pulled other people in behind him, and more of them turn up every month.

He reminds us that homelessness is not just an issue, it is a human experience, and that everyone deserves kindness and opportunity. Change starts with one person choosing to care. Thank you, Charlie. You care so much.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to recognize the enduring significance of the Battle of Vimy Ridge, fought on April 9, 1917, one of the defining moments in Canada's history. Since 2006, the Vimy Foundation has been dedicated to raising awareness and educating Canadians about the battle. This year's campaign marks the beginning of the lead-up to the 110th anniversary of the battle in 2027.

My colleague from across the floor said last week that we are "a country that forgets too easily." I do not think he is wrong. That is what Vimy Week is for, and it runs this year from April 2 to April 9.

I encourage all members of this House to wear the Vimy Pin. The pin is composed of four distinct colours, and it symbolizes the unity and the sacrifice of the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge. I have pins here with me, and I will pass them to both sides of the Chamber before we rise.

By wearing it, we honour their courage, their sacrifice, and the legacy they left behind, a legacy that helped define our nation. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, our government has presented the 2026-27 capital budget. It is $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year. That is the largest capital budget ever tabled in this province. Most of the investments will go to the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure to improve our roads, bridges, ferries and other essential infrastructure, and the health care sector will also see significant investments, both to modernize our medical equipment and to renovate hospitals that in some cases have not had serious work done on them in my lifetime. In education, the budget builds new schools in Shediac and Moncton. It upgrades several institutions elsewhere in the province. This is not extravagance. It is the backlog left by years of underinvestment, and it has to be paid down eventually. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, our government has tabled the 2026-27 capital budget, and it is a historic one: $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year, the largest this province has ever tabled. Most of that money goes to the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure. It pays for roads, bridges, ferries and the other essential infrastructure New Brunswickers use without thinking about it. Hospitals get their share too — new medical equipment, and renovations to the buildings themselves. Shediac gets a new school. So does Moncton. Several other institutions around the province get upgrades. We did not invent this backlog. Governments underinvested for years, and someone has to pay that down. These investments keep people safe, they make life better here, and they leave our communities something to work with. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, employees must have at least 90 days of continuous employment to be eligible for the leave, which aligns with leave provisions in other provinces. They are required to inform the employer as soon as possible of their need for leave. Employers may require reasonable medical documentation confirming that the employee is unable to work due to illness or injury. Those elements support the integrity of the leave and give employers reasonable assurance and predictability. A member stopped me in the hallway this morning with three questions and I will put them on the record. What happens to a seasonal worker who is 80 days in? Who pays for the note from the doctor? Does a nurse practitioner's signature count as medical documentation? I don't have those answers today. This amendment strengthens protections for workers when they are most vulnerable, while keeping a balanced approach that considers the realities of workplaces across the province. No one should have to choose between their health and their job. It addresses a clear gap in our current legislation, and it keeps a reasonable, structured approach for employers. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

The strain on our labour relations has become undeniable, and it is casting a shadow over the collective effort to build prosperity in New Brunswick. I think this government's legislative approach has fallen short, and we ought to acknowledge that. Going forward, we should prioritize genuine dialogue, transparency, and mutual respect in our dealings with workers and their representatives. Trust is built that way or it is not built at all.

Mr. Speaker, in December 2019, this Legislature was embroiled in a contentious debate over essential service legislation, specifically about the wages of nursing home workers. Honestly, I am not an arbitrator and I have never sat at a bargaining table, so I will not pretend to know the mechanics of it better than the people who lived it. What I do know is that Bill 17 imposed conditions on how labour arbitrators could rule on the wages of these workers, and that members of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions voiced their opposition and expressed their concern about the impact on their ability to strike and to negotiate a fair wage. Their protest underscored the depth of their discontent.

The law passed. Union leaders decried it as an attack on public-sector labour unions. Sharon Teare, President of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions, avowed that their voice would not be silenced, and she emphasized their commitment to fighting for better working conditions and to protecting the rights of nursing home workers, who play a valuable role in our society. I have read her remarks. I would not want to be on the other side of them.

Bill 17 highlighted the ongoing tension between the government and labour unions in this province, particularly on labour rights and collective bargaining. It underscored the challenge in balancing the interests of workers against those of taxpayers and against the government's fiscal responsibility. I do not know where the line sits. I am not sure anyone in here does.

But when we reflect on December 2019 and the passage of Bill 17, we cannot forget that there are members of this government today who were opposed to that bill. They vocally expressed their discontent. They said they would stand with labour movements as long as they could. That has changed today.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association are in the gallery this afternoon, and among them are members of the association's Board of Directors. A member opposite asked across the floor a moment ago who exactly was upstairs, so let me be exact: this is the board, not a delegation. Their work supporting the mental health and well-being of New Brunswickers is essential. The association continues to work with the Department of Health, and that collaboration is helping to strengthen our system of care. I will say more about that later today, when we get to statements by ministers. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

As New Brunswickers gather around their Christmas trees this year, they'll be exchanging more than just presents. They'll be swapping stories about how the Holt government has turned its promises into ornaments — sparkly, shiny, and completely hollow. We hear the word "discipline" a lot from the other side of this House. I've written it down three times this week. First there was the balanced budget promise, the one we were told would be delivered with fanfare and a drumroll. Instead, what do we have? A deficit under the tree. It's not even the gift that keeps on giving. It's the gift that keeps on taking. Then there's the carbon tax adjustor, which the members opposite keep describing as "a technical matter." It is a promise so simple it could have been done with the stroke of a pen. Instead, it's still there, adding to the prices of everything we buy every day. That's not the Christmas cheer we were hoping for. New Brunswickers have been promised a lot of things. This government needs to realize that promises aren't just for the Christmas season. They're for the whole year. It's time they deliver.

Madam Speaker, on October 24, our community celebrated the 105th birthday of Ms. Laura Anderson of Newtown. Laura is remarkable - strong, vibrant, still living independently in her own home. She had her driver's licence until just this past month and still enjoyed short drives on the rural roads she knows so well. Laura and her late husband, Thomas, were pioneers in agriculture and in tourism in this province. They were founding members of the Agricultural Museum of New Brunswick. In 1967, the centennial year, they launched New Brunswick's very first farm vacation experience. Families and travellers came from across the province and from around the world. Laura still shares her humour, her stories and her wisdom, and she has been doing it for 105 years now. Congratulations, Laura, and thank you.

Madam Deputy Speaker, I have never worked a shift in a nursing home, and I would not stand here and tell this House I know what that job takes. What I do know is how those workers were treated under Premier Higgs. They were taken to court. They were told they could relocate to Alberta if they wanted better wages. That was a failure in negotiation and it was a betrayal of the people who provide essential care to our most vulnerable, and it showed a lack of empathy for those on the front lines. Then the school strike ran 16 days and was ended with emergency orders forcing workers back to work. I will grant that a government has to keep schools open. Here is what that looked like on the ground, though: bus drivers in Woodstock who had been out in the cold for two weeks went back with no agreement and no arbitration date. Watering down binding arbitration, scab-friendly legislation, and now this pension bill - it is a pattern, and it erodes the foundation of workers' rights. These decisions hit real livelihoods and the health of our communities, and it is our duty to question them. Madam Deputy Speaker, you will recall the unions expressing their vehement disagreement with the wage-freeze restriction mandate - the 0% mandate in the early years of this government. I do not have the transcript of that meeting in front of me, and I was not in the room. In the face of a global pandemic, our frontline workers were nothing short of heroes. Their commitment and their sacrifices demanded acknowledgement and tangible support. The union leaders rightly asserted that these heroes deserved more than zeroes in their wage agreements.

We are building a system where mental health care and addiction care work hand in hand. Honestly, I am not a clinician and I have never worked in addictions treatment, so I am relying here on the people who do. What they tell me is that these challenges are usually connected in the same person and have to be addressed together.

So we are integrating the services, and the province is creating a seamless continuum of care that spans prevention, treatment, recovery, and harm reduction. That gets people the right supports at every stage of their journey. For children and youth, it means early community-based interventions that can prevent substance use from escalating and reduce long-term harms. For someone already living with addiction, it means timely access to a full range of treatment options: detox services, live-in programs, outpatient counselling, and long-term recovery supports.

Our investments reflect this. The Moncton Addictions and Mental Health Court will offer those facing mental health and addiction challenges an opportunity to access treatment and community supports when they come into contact with the justice system. It gives someone facing criminal charges an alternative pathway to traditional sentencing, connecting them to treatment and recovery supports while easing pressures on the justice system and improving long-term outcomes for participants.

This week we took the first step to expand treatment capacity, and we announced a new 50-bed addiction treatment facility. Is 50 enough? I don't know. I doubt it. We are actively exploring further opportunities to increase the number of treatment beds across New Brunswick.

Well, beds are no good without staff. That is why there are 10 newly established trainer positions dedicated to building the skills, expertise, and resilience of the addictions and mental health workforce. Together, these efforts will strengthen service delivery, create consistency across the province, and help ensure people living with substance use challenges receive the right care at the right time and in the right setting.

Madam Speaker, last September we started a universal breakfast program in every school in New Brunswick. It has been close to a year, and we can see what it does. Students eat in the morning now: milk, eggs, bagels, apples, cheese, and, in one school I was in, a pan of leftover baked beans. FeedNB works with the schools, and much of the food comes off farms and out of businesses here at home. Parents tell us the program saves them time and money, and it takes some of the noise out of the house at seven in the morning. That counts for more when groceries cost what they cost now. A child who has eaten can sit down and learn something. That is what we paid for. Every child should be able to start the day fed, Madam Speaker. Thank you.

Madam Deputy Speaker, Premier Higgs took nursing home workers to court. He told them to go to Alberta if they wanted better wages. Those are the people who lift our parents out of bed, who feed them, who sit with them at the end. A premier who says that to them has not failed at negotiating. He has told them what he thinks they are worth.

The school strike lasted 16 days. It ended when this government signed emergency orders and ordered the workers back into the buildings. A government cannot say it believes in bargaining and in the right to strike and then do that.

This government watered down binding arbitration. It brought in scab-friendly legislation. Now it brings us this pension bill. Custodians, bus drivers, educational assistants, laundry staff, and the woman who does the payroll for all of them — every one of them loses a little more ground each time.

Madam Deputy Speaker, you will recall the unions and their vehement disagreement with the wage-freeze restriction mandate this government proposed in its early years. Zero percent. In a global pandemic, our frontline workers were heroes, and this government offered them zero. They earned more than a round of applause from this Chamber. They earned money. The union leaders said it better than I will: these heroes deserved more than zeroes.

When a government decides these things, somebody's mortgage moves. Somebody's daughter takes the job in Fort McMurray. We are here to question that, and I question it. A fair society lets a worker bargain across the table as an equal, and this one has spent five years making sure she cannot.

Mr. Speaker, this is a government that took nursing home workers to court. That is where we ended up — the Premier in a courtroom against the people who bathe and feed our parents, and then telling them, when they gathered outside, to go to Alberta if they wanted better wages.

The offer on the table was 10.5 cents an hour. Ten and a half cents. On a 37.5-hour week that is $3.94, and something like $205 over a year, in a year when Statistics Canada had grocery prices running 10% to 11% above the year before. Those two numbers do not sit beside each other honestly.

Then came binding arbitration with conditions attached, which is not arbitration. The conditions were the point. Attaching them was a way to keep the workers' actual demands off the table before anybody sat down at it.

His words to the protesters were, "if you want that kind of wage, then Alberta's where to get it." That is dismissive, and it ignores what these workers are up against here. Instead of dealing with what was in front of him, the Premier deflected.

And he told us that fair wages would not fix the staffing shortage in our nursing homes. A fair wage is a matter of justice for the worker, yes. It is also the recruitment and retention tool the province has been refusing to pick up.

He never treated it as urgent. He never sat down with them in any meaningful way. His responsibility is to the people of New Brunswick, and we are going to keep reminding him of it.

Madam Speaker, the aim of this bill is to make things easier, not to approve them. It removes barriers. It provides clarity. It puts New Brunswick in a position to move forward when the time comes. The proposal was drafted in consultation with several departments, including the Office of the Attorney General, Service New Brunswick, the Department of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, and the Department of Indigenous Affairs. The NB Power Board of Directors will continue to oversee all security measures, ensuring financial accountability and risk mitigation. The information will be used as the basis of the proposal submitted for government approval, and it will be reviewed before any authorization. I am going to say that one more time, because I have been asked about it twice today: it will be reviewed before any authorization. Madam Speaker, the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future — a bold and necessary investment. This bill ensures that we are prepared to meet its challenges with the flexibility, clarity, and confidence required. I urge all members of the House to support the bill and help us take the next step toward securing clean energy for New Brunswickers, today and for decades to come. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Employees need 90 days of continuous employment to be eligible for the leave. That lines up with the leave provisions in other provinces. They have to tell their employer as soon as possible that they need it, and the employer may require reasonable medical documentation confirming that the employee is unable to work due to illness or injury. That is not a hurdle. It keeps the leave sound, and it gives the employer something to plan around, which matters a great deal to a small operator who has to cover a shift on short notice for the better part of half a year. Madam Speaker, this amendment is a step forward. It strengthens protections for workers at the time they are most vulnerable, and it does that without ignoring what workplaces across this province actually look like. It also keeps New Brunswick a place where people can live and work with dignity. No one should have to choose between their health and their job. There is a clear gap in our current legislation. This closes it. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I thank the Minister of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour for his statement on the InnovateNB Awards, and I join him in recognizing this year's recipients. They are pushing boundaries and driving progress in this province, and that deserves the House's notice. The minister used the phrase "growing confidence" in New Brunswick's business climate. I wrote it down. Growing where, and for whom? I would put it to him that confidence is not shared equally across all sectors and communities, and I've heard the member for Campbellton-Dalhousie say much the same thing in this Chamber twice this fall. Innovation does not exist in a vacuum. It requires a supportive ecosystem, and the barriers many innovators face here have not moved. Our rural areas still struggle to access the resources and the support that urban centres enjoy. The benefits have to reach every corner of the province and not just those with established networks. The recipients are inspiring, but I want to ask the minister what we are doing to cultivate the next generation. Investments in education, mentorship programs, and accessible funds are essential if our youth are going to lead the charge. And while we celebrate, we still need continued investment in research and development, particularly in clean technology and sustainable practices, the sectors that align with the economic goals this government has set out. When the estimates for the department come before the Committee of Supply, I intend to ask about exactly that. Government, industry, and communities working together is the only way an inclusive environment gets built. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Too often, the subsidies and the incentives go to large corporations. Not to the small and medium-sized businesses that create most of the local jobs in our communities. That is backwards. Direct that investment to smaller businesses instead and the wealth generated by economic activity stays in New Brunswick communities, in the towns where it was earned in the first place. One idea that has been suggested is stronger support for community economic development corporations, which allow residents to invest directly in businesses by purchasing community investment shares. Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have done it. Hundreds of enterprises have been launched under those models, including renewable energy projects and community-based ventures. It works. With provincial support and promotion, it could work here too. Citizens raised energy as well. The message was not complicated. Stop leaning on large, high-risk megaprojects. There is growing support for a diversified approach focused on efficiency and renewables: an energy investment fund to help new technologies reach commercialization, a modest levy on electrical bills dedicated to efficiency and renewable projects, and a Property Assessed Clean Energy program to fund solar installations, battery storage and efficiency upgrades. Household costs would come down. Skilled jobs would go up. And the long-term electrical demand challenge NB Power is facing gets a little easier, which is not a sentence I get to say often in this Chamber. Then there is procurement. Every year the provincial government spends tens of millions of dollars on goods and services. Much of that money leaves. It goes to large corporations, or to suppliers outside this province, and it does not come back. Send even a small portion of it to local businesses, cooperatives and social enterprises and you have created something real. Hospitals, universities, schools and correctional facilities buy much the same things year after year. Redirect a small share of those contracts and it ripples.

Madam Speaker, my colleague across the way said a few minutes ago that this bill will "approve the Mactaquac project." That is not what is in front of us at second reading. The bill's aim is to make things easier, not to approve them. It removes barriers, it provides clarity, and it makes sure New Brunswick is prepared to move forward when the time comes. On the consultation point the member raised: the proposal was drafted with the Office of the Attorney General, Service New Brunswick, the Department of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, and the Department of Indigenous Affairs. The NB Power Board of Directors will continue to oversee all security measures — and "continue" is the word I want on the record, because financial accountability and risk mitigation do not move anywhere. The information will be used as the basis of the proposal submitted for government approval, and it will be reviewed before any authorization. The Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future, and this bill ensures we are prepared to meet its challenges with the flexibility, clarity, and confidence required. I urge all members to support the bill and take the next step toward securing clean energy for New Brunswickers, today and for decades to come. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise today with great satisfaction and deep gratitude. After years of waiting, the new, hoped-for bridge between Île Lamèque and Shippagan will be built.

I will be honest with the House. I did not think I would be standing here saying that. I have said in this Chamber before that I had given up on it, and I was wrong.

I thank the Premier, Hon. Susan Holt, and the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure, Hon. Chuck Chiasson, for coming to the region in February and making that announcement, which marks a turning point for our communities. The bridge will simplify travel, strengthen our connections with the rest of the province, and bring new economic opportunities to our people.

I don't know the engineering side of it and I'm not going to pretend I do. But on behalf of my constituents, I want to express our gratitude to everyone who played a role in making this important project happen. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association are in the gallery today, and several of them sit on the association's Board of Directors. A few of them travelled from as far as Bathurst to get here for two o'clock. Their work holds up mental health and well-being in this province. The association keeps working with the Department of Health, and our system of care is stronger for that. There is more to say about it, and I will say it later today. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I learned this week that Roméo H. LeBlanc has died. He was 102. He was an Acadian, and he was a veteran of the Second World War. As Minister responsible for Military Affairs, I want to pay tribute to him for his exceptional service to our country.

The war was not the end of it. For the decades after he came home he stayed with the veterans' community, showing up for the men and women who had served, and making sure that the ones who did not come back were still spoken about by name at the Legion and in his own town. Courage, devotion, a deep sense of duty. He had all of it, and he would have waved it off if you said so. He would have.

On behalf of the government of New Brunswick, I extend my sincerest condolences to his family, his loved ones, and the entire veterans' community. We will remember him. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. As the holiday season comes on, I rise to talk about shopping local.

Small businesses are the heartbeat of New Brunswick's economy. They are the cafes and restaurants where neighbours gather, the boutiques and artisans that bring character to our downtowns, and the family-owned shops passed down through generations. They are the local producers who remind us that world-class quality is made right here at home. They are employers, they hold up their communities, and they are a real part of the economic development of this province.

When we choose to shop locally, particularly during the holidays, we are doing more than purchasing a gift. We are investing directly in our communities. For every dollar spent locally, more of that dollar stays right here in New Brunswick, creating jobs, supporting local supply chains and strengthening our regional economies. Honestly, I'm not an economist, and I couldn't tell you the exact multiplier. I do know what it looks like on a main street when the money stays.

At the Premier's open house yesterday, the turnout was strong and the vendors were a genuinely varied bunch. I'll admit I went in expecting the same faces I always see. I was wrong. I spoke to one vendor who started his business at nine years old.

So go to the markets this holiday season. Visit a neighbourhood shop you have walked past for years. Find the artisans, and choose New Brunswick-made products and services where you can. The choices are small, and they add up, and by supporting local shopping we're supporting the people who support us all year.

A special thank-you to everyone who was out yesterday and who spoke to those vendors.

Madam Speaker, a new provincial website went live this week: artsculturenb.ca. It puts artists, artisans and the places you can go and see them in one spot, and it arrived just in time for the holiday season.

A New Brunswicker hunting for a gift can find one on it — a print, a concert ticket, a bowl, a Saturday market two towns over. Artists and organizations post their own events and their own work on the site themselves. Nobody has to ask us first.

We built it so that more people know what is being made here, get out to see it, and pay for it. I encourage everyone to visit artsculturenb.ca and see what this province is making.

This holiday season, let's encourage local shopping, celebrate our local talent, and support the artists who make our province extraordinary. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I'll be honest with the House — I am not a transportation planner, and I had to go back and read the 2017 report again before I put this motion on the order paper. From Surfaces to Services. It said this province needed a comprehensive, coordinated approach to public transportation. That was 2017. Nothing meaningful has been done since.

Whose desk is it on? I don't know. That is the whole problem. Nobody owns the file, so nobody answers for it. Give one minister a mandate and somebody has to answer for the leadership, the coordination, the money, the way the pieces connect, and the schedules that never line up.

Be it therefore resolved that this Legislative Assembly urge the Premier to give the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure a mandate for public transportation; and be it further resolved that this Assembly urge government to allocate the resources and the funding the New Brunswick Transportation Authority needs to create a public transportation strategy and to implement it.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the minister's statement on the InnovateNB Awards. It is an occasion to celebrate the people who are pushing boundaries and driving progress in New Brunswick, and I congratulate this year's recipients. But no innovator works in a vacuum. Someone has to build the ecosystem around them, and this province still puts barriers in the way of people who are trying. The minister told the House that businesses have a growing confidence in New Brunswick's climate. Not every business shares it. A machine shop in Doaktown, a software firm in Moncton, a boat builder on the Acadian Peninsula, a woodlot operator, a nurse practitioner running her own clinic — they do not all get at the same programs on the same terms. Rural applicants cannot reach the resources and the supports that people in the urban centres reach. Innovation has to pay off in every corner of this province, not only for the people who already know whom to call. This year's recipients inspire me. But who is coming after them? We equip our youth by funding schools, by pairing them with mentors, and by opening funds they can actually get at. And the departments have to keep putting money into research and development, particularly in clean technology and sustainable practices, which is where our economic goals point. Let government, industry, and communities do this together, and let us leave nobody out. Our future depends on it. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

The bill empowers the minister to require health care organizations to implement improvement plans. Accountability matters, and I'm not going to stand here and argue against it. What worries me is centralization. Health care organizations operate in vastly different environments, such as urban hospitals, rural facilities, community clinics, and long-term care settings. A one-size-fits-all approach imposed from the centre may not reflect local realities. In Perth-Andover the nurse practitioner covers three villages and does her own scheduling; a plan written on Queen Street will not know that. Ministerial authority should support improvement rather than replace professional judgment. Oversight should guide, not micromanage.

Perhaps the most serious issue lies in subsection 6.2. It says that if the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act conflicts with the Right to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, this Act prevails. That is a significant legal step. Government members are effectively creating an exception to one of the most core privacy protections governing public institutions. I am not a lawyer, and I would welcome being told I have this wrong. But I read subsection 6.2 four times last night and that is what it says.

The government argues that confidentiality encourages open discussion during safety reviews. There is merit to that. Health care professionals must feel safe speaking candidly. Overriding existing privacy legislation still demands rigorous justification. What could be withheld, from whom, with what appeal? Too much secrecy undermines public trust. Too little discourages honest reporting. This clause deserves detailed committee scrutiny.

The bill also expands rules allowing the disclosure of incident reports and improvement findings. System-wide learning is a good objective. Disclosure frameworks still have to protect patient identity. My fear is that information flows upward into bureaucracy and never reaches the front-line practitioners who could prevent the next one. Learning has to travel across the system, not just up into reports.

One theme runs through the bill: administration. New committees, new reporting obligations, new procedural requirements. Administration is not inherently negative. But every hour spent preparing reports is an hour not spent with patients, and the government has to show these additions will measurably improve care outcomes. Otherwise we are adding weight to a system already struggling.

Bill 40 amends the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act. That Act already sets up a framework for reviewing patient safety incidents and learning from them. The government says the amendments will improve how health care incidents are reviewed, strengthen collaboration, make reviews more consistent, and improve transparency for patients and families. Nobody is going to stand up and oppose that. But a bill is not judged by what it intends. It is judged by what it does.

So I want to put some questions to the minister. What specific problem is this bill trying to fix? Are incident reviews not happening now? Are the lessons not being shared? Are patients not being told? Are the health authorities ignoring recommendations? We raised this at the briefing on the bill. Those answers are not clearly provided.

Legislative change should follow a demonstrated gap. The government has not put forward data showing a systemic failure under the current law. Without that, we are legislating in search of a problem rather than solving one. Diagnosis before treatment.

The biggest change here is a new body, the New Brunswick Quality of Care and Patient Safety Advisory Committee, established and maintained by the minister. On paper, who could oppose expert advice on patient safety? Here is where I would slow down. Health care professionals in this province already answer to Horizon Health Network, Vitalité Health Network, professional regulatory colleges, accreditation bodies, internal quality review committees, and patient advocacy offices. Is this improving outcomes? Is it another layer? Which of those bodies gets wound up when this one starts? I don't know. Front-line workers already tell us they spend more and more of the day filling out forms instead of caring for patients. If this committee becomes one more reporting layer with no measurable improvement, we will have worsened the very system we set out to help.

Madam Speaker, I want to start by recognizing that this bill brings forward some long-overdue clarifications. It updates outdated language, replacing legal Latin with plain English. That might seem minor, but clarity matters. It also simplifies the processes for brewers and distillers to sell their products at what the bill calls "approved farmers' markets" — and I would like the minister to tell the committee who does the approving. Small producers in New Brunswick have been asking for this. When a microbrewery or a craft distillery can connect directly with customers at the Saint Andrews farmers' market, the St. George market, or the market in St. Stephen, it helps drive tourism, encourages entrepreneurship, and strengthens local economies. I applaud that part of the bill.

The minister used the word "modernization" a few minutes ago. I'll use it too, but modernization should never come without scrutiny. This bill sets production caps: 500 000 L for brewers, and 75 000 L for distillers. That is when they are "operating as agents under the New Brunswick Liquor Corporation." Those are the bill's words, not mine, and "as agents" is doing a great deal of work in that clause. Now, those sound like fair limits. Were these caps determined in consultation with our smaller producers or primarily with larger operators? Will this inadvertently favour those already established in the market, making it harder for start-ups to grow into the next tier?

We've seen this before, where well-intentioned changes to regulation end up benefitting those with deeper pockets and more connections, while small business owners struggle with compliance costs and licencing delays. Craft producers in St. Croix and elsewhere in New Brunswick, people who pour their life savings into starting a brewery or a distillery, say: We don't mind rules, but we just want fair ones.

This is my question for the government: How will fairness between small and large producers be ensured under this new licencing model?

Madam Speaker, I'm delighted to announce that we have launched a new provincial website for the arts, culture, and creative industries in New Brunswick. It's called artsculturenb.ca, and it's here just in time for the holiday season. The site puts our artists, our artisans, and our cultural experiences in one place: a printmaker in Sackville, a fiddler with three dates before Christmas, a pottery studio that runs Saturday classes, a theatre company, a woman who carves birds. New Brunswickers looking for a gift, a show, or something to do on a Friday night can find it there and put their money into our creative sector at the same time. People working in the sector post their own events and creations to it. They don't need our permission and they don't need our help. I encourage everyone to visit artsculturenb.ca. This holiday season, let's shop local, celebrate our talent, and support the artists who make our province extraordinary. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to recognize the enduring significance of the Battle of Vimy Ridge, fought on April 9, 1917, one of the defining moments in Canada's history. I am not a historian, and I would not pretend to be one in this House. But I know what the date means. Since 2006, the Vimy Foundation has been dedicated to raising awareness and educating Canadians about the battle, and this year's campaign marks the beginning of the lead-up to the 110th anniversary of the Battle of Vimy Ridge in 2027. As we approach Vimy Week, from April 2 to 9, I encourage all members of this House to wear the Vimy Pin. It is composed of four distinct colours, and it symbolizes the unity and sacrifice of the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge. I had to be told that about the colours. Now I know. By wearing it, we honour their courage, their sacrifice, and the legacy they left behind, a legacy that helped define our nation. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

This approach lets the province put its own money and its own people back on the work only the province can do, and lets private practices handle the routine calls, because that is where the expertise already sits. We are not walking away. We want a model that is more modern, that lasts, and that lines up with how the rest of Canada does this, so that a farmer can still get a vet who knows what is coming at that farm now and in ten years. New Brunswick can build that model around what farms actually need, and the quality of the work does not have to drop to do it. We know the change is worrying people. In remote regions, producers are asking what a call will cost and who will answer it, and in several of those regions they were already waiting too long before we touched anything. So we are building a support program for private sector veterinarians. It will offset costs such as travel, so a producer in Restigouche can get the same visit as a producer twenty minutes from Sussex. What we have said so far has not settled every worry. It does show that we mean to fix these things case by case. The labs matter here. Our labs catch an emerging disease early, they stop an outbreak before it moves, and they keep the food supply safe, and every existing lab stays open through the whole transition so that no farmer and no veterinarian loses a day's work waiting on a result. We still have to agree on this, and I want to hear your opinions, your ideas, and your worries. This is a big change, and it will only work if the people it lands on decide to take part.

Bill 40 proposes significant amendments to the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act. That Act already establishes a framework for reviewing and learning from patient safety incidents. According to the government, the amendments aim to improve how health care incidents are reviewed, strengthen collaboration, enhance consistency and improve transparency for patients and families. Those are worthy objectives. No reasonable person opposes a system that learns better and communicates better with the families who need to hear from it.

But legislation is not judged by its intentions. It is judged by its consequences.

So, before we create new structures or grant new powers, what specific problem is this bill trying to address? The Act already provides a framework for patient safety reviews. What has failed? Are incident reviews not occurring? Are lessons not being shared? Are patients not being informed? These concerns were raised during the briefing on the bill, and rightfully so, because legislative changes ought to follow a demonstrated gap and the government has not put clear data in front of this House showing a systemic failure under the current law. Without that, we are legislating in search of a problem. Diagnosis comes before treatment.

Bill 40 also creates a New Brunswick Quality of Care and Patient Safety Advisory Committee, established and maintained by the minister. On paper that sounds fine. Who could oppose expert advice on patient safety?

Here is where we should slow down. Health care professionals in this province already operate within Horizon Health Network, Vitalite Health Network, professional regulatory colleges, accreditation bodies, internal quality review committees and patient advocacy offices, and every one of those structures generates paperwork that somebody in scrubs has to fill out at the end of a shift. Front-line workers are telling us they spend more time on forms than on patients. Are we improving outcomes, or are we adding bureaucracy? If this committee is one more reporting layer with nothing measurable behind it, we will have made the system worse. That is my worry.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I want to talk about labour relations in New Brunswick. Workers make their living inside those relations, and the economy of this province grows or stalls with them, so this matters to everyone in this Chamber. Over the last few years the Higgs government and the labour movement have fallen into a troubling pattern. The government has not sat down with workers and their representatives to talk and to bargain. It has legislated instead. Bill 23 in 2022. Bill 17 last fall. The essential service legislation this House debated in December 2019. Three separate times, this government settled a labour question inside the Legislative Assembly rather than at a table with New Brunswick workers sitting across from it. It did not consult the unions properly and it did not work with them, and the distance between this government and the people who do the work has widened every time. Each one of those bills was a chance the government let go by. The amendments to the Public Service Labour Relations Act were a chance. The change to the essential service legislation was a chance. Employers and employees have to trust one another to get anything done, and this government has spent that trust down to very little. Workers across the province feel it. Nurses feel it, snowplow operators feel it, the people who answer the phones at Service New Brunswick feel it, and so do the folks in the yards in Edmundston. They are disillusioned. Morale in the workforce has dropped, and our industries are less productive and worse off for it.

Madam Speaker, on October 24, in Newtown, we marked the 105th birthday of Ms. Laura Anderson. Laura is strong, she is vibrant, and she is still living independently in her own home. She held a valid driver's licence until just this past month, which is a bit over 88 years after she got her first one, and she was still taking short drives on the rural roads she knows so well. Laura and her late husband, Thomas, were true pioneers in this province's agricultural and tourism sectors. They were founding members of the Agricultural Museum of New Brunswick, and that museum has done as much as any body in this province to preserve our farming heritage. In 1967, Canada's centennial year, they opened New Brunswick's very first farm vacation experience. Families and travellers came from across the province and from around the world, and they kept coming for decades. Laura still shares her humour, her stories and her advice, whether or not you asked for it. Congratulations on 105 years, Laura, and thank you.

Too often the subsidies and the economic development incentives go to large corporations, not to the small and medium-sized businesses that create most of the local jobs in our communities. Put that money into the smaller shops and the wealth generated by economic activity stays here. It stays in the community that generated it.

The people who came to our sessions kept coming back to community economic development corporations. Residents buy community investment shares and put their money directly into a business down the road from them. Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have launched hundreds of enterprises this way — wind projects, a fish plant, community-based ventures, a bakery. If the province backed the model and promoted it, entrepreneurs here could use it too, and small places could hold onto the businesses they start.

The same people want the province to modernize how it thinks about energy. They are not asking for another large, high-risk megaproject. They want efficiency and renewables, spread across a lot of smaller bets. Set up an energy investment fund so a new technology can get to commercialization. Put a modest levy on electrical bills and dedicate it to efficiency and renewable projects. Run a Property Assessed Clean Energy program that pays for solar installations, battery storage, new windows, insulation, heat pumps. Households would pay less for power. Tradespeople would get skilled work. NB Power would face less of the long-term electrical demand it keeps warning us about.

Finally, citizens want the province to spend its own money closer to home. Government buys tens of millions of dollars of goods and services every year, and much of that currently goes to large corporations or to suppliers outside this province. Send even a small portion to local businesses, to cooperatives, to social enterprises, and you have created real opportunity in communities across New Brunswick. Hospitals, universities, schools, correctional facilities — they know what they will need to buy next year and the year after. Redirect a small share of those contracts on purpose and the money moves through the whole province.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in sadness on the passing of Robert Hosford, beloved husband, father, pop pop, uncle, great-uncle, and friend. Robert passed away on Wednesday, November 12. I did not know him nearly as well as many of the people who will be in that room this week, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. But I know what his family has told me. He left behind a legacy of love, laughter, and adventure. He was a devoted family man and the cornerstone of his family, always putting their needs before his own. His love and support knew no bounds, and he was always there to lend a helping hand or offer a listening ear. I am told that warm smile and that infectious laugh could light up a room. His sense of humour could turn even the toughest day into a memorable moment. Robert was his family's biggest cheerleader, proudly supporting their endeavours and celebrating their success. Whether he was cheering on his favourite team or teaching a lesson, his passion for sports was only matched by his love for his family. Please join me in expressing condolences to Robert's family and friends. Thank you.

Madam Speaker, I want to recognize Nursing Home Without Walls. The program makes a real difference for seniors in our communities. Bill 40 proposes significant amendments to the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act. That Act already sets up a framework for reviewing and learning from patient safety incidents. According to the government, the amendments aim to improve how health care incidents are reviewed, strengthen collaboration, enhance consistency, and improve transparency for patients and families. Those are worthy objectives. No reasonable person opposes a system that learns better.

But legislation is judged by its consequences, not its intentions, and as we examine Bill 40 closely, several questions arise. Before we create new structures or grant new powers: what specific problem is this bill trying to address? The existing Act already provides a framework for patient safety reviews, so what has failed? Are incident reviews not occurring? Are lessons not being shared? Are patients not being informed? Are health authorities ignoring recommendations? These concerns were raised during the briefing, and rightfully so. Legislative changes should follow demonstrated gaps. The government has not presented clear data showing a systemic failure under the current law. Without that, we risk legislating in search of a problem rather than solving one.

One of the most significant changes is the creation of a New Brunswick Quality of Care and Patient Safety Advisory Committee, to be established and maintained by the minister. On paper this sounds reasonable. Who could oppose expert advice on patient safety?

Here is where prudence requires us to slow down. Health care professionals in this province already operate within multiple oversight structures: Horizon, Vitalite, the colleges, accreditation bodies, internal quality review committees, patient advocacy offices. I was at the Chalmers in February. The staff there did not ask me for another committee. They are already telling us they spend increasing amounts of time filling out forms instead of caring for patients. If this becomes another reporting layer without measurable improvement, we will have unintentionally worsened the very system we set out to protect.

Hands-on help. A senior needs two things to walk in there and come out with an account: a Medicare card and an email address. That is it.
