Property owners pay the cost of assessment fee on the property tax bill, and that fee goes through Finance and Treasury Board. Property owners also pay charges through their local tax rates. So the same owner is paying twice, directly and indirectly. First, the Finance and Treasury Board cost of assessment fee printed on the tax bill. Second, the municipal taxes that are used to pay Service New Brunswick for assessment services.

Madam Speaker, most New Brunswickers do not know that. They look at the one visible charge on the bill and assume that is the entirety of the assessment cost. They do not realize that the municipality is paying Service New Brunswick as well.

I want to be absolutely clear about something. This motion does not criticize the work performed by Service New Brunswick. Assessment services are necessary. Municipalities require accurate assessments, and Service New Brunswick provides an actual service to municipalities and to rural districts. Finance and Treasury Board is not providing assessment services. Finance and Treasury Board is charging the cost of assessment fee directly through the property tax bill, and that is the charge this motion seeks to eliminate. After years of rising assessments and rising costs, the time has come to do it.

I brought my own notice with me. Mine went up somewhere around 11% to 12% in a single year, against 3% or so the year before that. That figure is off my kitchen table, not out of the department, and I would welcome the minister correcting it with the departmental number.

No homeowner asked for property values to surge. No senior on a fixed income requested that a modest house be reassessed at a dramatically higher value, and we all know that assessments have gone up in recent years. With COVID-19 and people moving to New Brunswick, home prices went up, and fair market value is a big factor in the assessment process. That is why the increase was what it was. Every time an assessment rises, the government's revenue from this fee rises with it. That creates a perception, and it is a troubling one: that government benefits financially from the very increases that keep a woman on a fixed income awake at two in the morning.

Employees must have at least 90 days of continuous employment to be eligible for the leave, which aligns with leave provisions in other provinces. Employees are required to inform their employer as soon as possible of their need for leave. Employers may also require reasonable medical documentation confirming that the employee is unable to work due to illness or injury. That is not a hurdle. It gives an employer some assurance and some predictability about who is coming back and when, and it keeps the leave from being something other than what this House intended it to be. Madam Speaker, this amendment is an important step forward. It strengthens protections for workers at a time when they are most vulnerable, and it does that while taking account of what workplaces across this province actually look like — a garage with four employees, a call centre with four hundred, a farm where the season does not wait for anybody's recovery. New Brunswick should be a place where people can live and work with dignity. No one should have to choose between their health and their job. This amendment addresses a clear gap in our legislation. It is a practical step. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. The holiday season is nearly here, and I rise to talk about supporting our local businesses at the time of year when our communities are shining brighter than ever. Small businesses are the heartbeat of New Brunswick's economy. I mean the cafes and restaurants where neighbours gather, the boutiques and artisans that give our downtowns their character, the family-owned shops passed down through generations, and the local producers who remind us that world-class quality is made right here at home. They are not only storefronts. They are employers, they support their communities, and they are essential contributors to the economic development of this province.

When we choose to shop locally, particularly during the holidays, we are doing more than purchasing a gift. We are investing directly in our communities. For every dollar spent locally, more of that dollar stays right here in New Brunswick, creating jobs, supporting local supply chains and strengthening our regional economies. I'm not an economist, and I'm not going to stand here and put a number on that multiplier. But I saw the thing itself yesterday at the Premier's open house. So many vendors, and such a range of them. I spoke with one man who started his business when he was nine years old. Nine.

Well, that turnout told me two things. New Brunswickers want to buy local. And the talent in our small business community is remarkable. I encourage everyone to get out to the markets this season, visit the neighbourhood shops, find the artisans, and choose New Brunswick-made products and services. Choices big and small make a real difference, especially at this time of year. When we support local, we support the people who support us all year. I want to thank everyone who was out yesterday and took the time to speak with those vendors.

As New Brunswickers gather around their Christmas trees this year, they'll be exchanging more than just presents. Madam Deputy Speaker, the treatment of nursing home workers under Premier Higgs' leadership was concerning. Taking them to court and suggesting that they relocate to Alberta for better wages was not only a failure in negotiation but a betrayal of the individuals who provide essential care to our vulnerable populations. I was not in the room for those talks. I have read the filings and I have spoken with two workers from the home in my riding, and that is the extent of what I know first-hand. One of them, a personal support worker with 22 years in, told me she had already looked up the flights. Then there was the 16-day school strike and the subsequent use of emergency orders to force workers back to work, which raised real questions about this government's commitment to meaningful dialogue and to the right to strike. Watering down binding arbitration, introducing scab-friendly legislation, and now this pension bill: the pattern erodes the foundation of workers' rights. I am not a labour lawyer. I do not know whether the arbitration change would survive a court challenge and I will not pretend that I do. What I do know is that the decisions made in this building land on the livelihoods of countless individuals and on the health of our communities. You will recall the unions expressing their vehement disagreement with the wage-freeze restriction mandate, the 0% wage mandate in the early years of this government. In the face of a global pandemic, our frontline workers were nothing short of heroes. The union leaders rightly asserted that these heroes deserved more than zeroes in their wage agreements. I have never had a better line handed to me, and I did not write it.

So the province keeps its own veterinarians on the files only the province can handle, and private clinics take the routine calls. We are not walking away. We are building the model that most of the country already runs, so a farmer can still get a vet out to the barn this year and in ten years. We need people onside for this. I want to hear from the producers, from the vets, from the people who have written to my office and told me flatly that they think we are wrong. I want to start by recognizing that this bill brings forward some long-overdue clarifications. It updates outdated language, replacing legal Latin with plain English. That might seem minor, but clarity matters. I'll say that again: clarity matters. It also simplifies the processes for brewers and distillers to sell their products at approved farmers' markets, something that small producers in New Brunswick have been asking for. The ability of a microbrewery or craft distillery to connect directly with customers at a local market, whether it's the Saint Andrews farmers' market, the St. George market, or the market in St. Stephen, helps drive tourism, encourages entrepreneurship, and strengthens local economies. I applaud that part of the bill, Madam Speaker. It recognizes the growth of a sector that has truly taken off here in New Brunswick. That said, modernization should never come without scrutiny. This bill sets production caps for breweries and distilleries: 500 000 L for brewers, and 75 000 L for distillers. That's when they are operating as agents under the New Brunswick Liquor Corporation. Now, those sound like fair limits, but we need to ask: Were these caps determined in consultation with our smaller producers or primarily with larger operators? Will this inadvertently favour those already established in the market, making it harder for start-ups to grow into the next tier? We've seen this before — we've seen this before — where well-intentioned changes to regulation end up benefitting those with deeper pockets and more connections, while small business owners struggle with compliance costs and licencing delays. Craft producers in St. Croix and elsewhere in New Brunswick, people who pour their life savings into starting a brewery or a distillery, say: We don't mind rules, but we just want fair ones. We don't mind rules, but we just want fair ones. That is what they told me, and I am repeating it word for word. This is my question for the government: How will fairness between small and large producers be ensured under this new licencing model?

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I am pleased to welcome members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association, who are joining us in the gallery today. Among our guests are members of the association's board of directors. Their work is essential to the mental health and well-being of New Brunswickers. I will say that again: essential. The association's continued collaboration with the Department of Health is helping to strengthen our system of care, and I look forward to sharing more on that a little later today. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, this government took nursing home workers to court. I want to say that again, because I think people at home stopped believing it when they heard it the first time. This government took nursing home workers to court, and the Premier told them to go to Alberta if they wanted better wages.

His offer was 10.5 cents an hour. Ten and a half cents an hour. That is what the people who bathe and feed our parents were worth to him at the table.

Then came binding arbitration with conditions. Conditions. Attach conditions and you have not agreed to arbitration, you have written the answer in advance, and that is a way of never dealing with what those workers came to say.

The words to the protesters were, "if you want that kind of wage, then Alberta's where to get it." I repeat — "Alberta's where to get it." That was said out loud, in this province, to New Brunswickers doing that work.

And then he told us fair wages will not fix the staffing shortage in our nursing homes. A fair wage is justice for the worker, and it is also how you keep one. He never treated any of it as urgent.

His responsibility is to the people of New Brunswick. Not to Alberta. To the people of New Brunswick.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. WHEREAS the 2017 From Surfaces to Services report identified the critical need for a comprehensive, coordinated approach to improving public transportation across the province, yet no meaningful action has been taken — and I am going to say that one more time, because it is the entire motion: no meaningful action has been taken; WHEREAS appointing a Minister responsible for public transportation would provide the leadership, coordination and accountability needed to develop, fund and integrate public transportation services throughout New Brunswick; BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Legislative Assembly urge the Premier to give the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure a mandate for public transportation; BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Legislative Assembly urge the government to allocate the resources and funding necessary to support the New Brunswick Transportation Authority to create and implement a public transportation strategy.

A mandate. That is what we are asking for. A mandate.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Up in the gallery today are members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association, and several of them sit on that association's Board of Directors. They are welcome here. These are people who see New Brunswickers on the worst days those people will ever have, and the work they do holding up mental health and well-being in this province is not work the system could do without. It is essential. The association keeps working with the Department of Health, and that is strengthening our system of care. I will have more to say about that later today. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Bill 40 amends the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act, which already sets out how we review patient safety incidents and learn from them. The government says the amendments will improve those reviews, strengthen collaboration, make things more consistent and improve transparency for patients and families. I am not going to argue against any of that. But a bill gets judged on what it does, not on what it hoped to do.

Now, I am not a clinician. I have never sat on a quality review committee and I would not pretend to know how one runs from the inside. What I can read is the bill, and what I keep looking for in it is the problem. The existing Act already provides the framework. So what failed? At the briefing those questions were asked and they were fair ones. The government has not shown us data on a systemic failure under the current law. Without that we are legislating in search of a problem.

The largest change is the New Brunswick Quality of Care and Patient Safety Advisory Committee, established and maintained by the minister. On paper, fine. Who opposes expert advice?

But slow down. Professionals here already answer to Horizon, to Vitalité, to their colleges, to accreditation bodies, to internal quality review committees, to the patient advocate. I asked a nurse in Sussex in February how many separate incident forms she fills out and she started counting on her fingers and gave up at four. That is the answer I keep getting.

So I don't know whether this committee improves an outcome or adds a layer. I would like to be convinced. If it becomes one more place to file a report and nothing measurable changes, we will have added weight to a system that is already carrying too much of it, and the people who feel that weight are not in this Chamber.

Madam Speaker, the Act as written says the executive committee has no quorum unless the deputy head whose mandate has a direct impact on the economy is present. That person, or their delegate, is a non-voting member. The idea was economic alignment across government. What it has produced is scheduling trouble and delayed decisions whenever that deputy head cannot be there.

The amendment before the House is straightforward. Quorum becomes a simple majority of voting members present.

Members are entitled to ask what this costs us. How many meetings has the current rule actually lost us in the past two years? Three? A dozen? Is that even the thing holding this committee back? I do not have those numbers in front of me today.

What I can tell members is what the amendment does not do. It does not alter the composition of the executive committee. It does not alter the participation of the deputy head whose mandate has a direct impact on the economy. That individual remains a valued contributor to the committee's work.

We made the same change for the board of directors in 2021, when the "quorum" definition in this Act was simplified for the board. This brings the two into line.

The committee will be able to meet and conduct its business without unnecessary disruption. In a fast-paced economic environment, the ability to act swiftly and effectively matters. Opportunities New Brunswick will be better positioned to deliver programs, to respond to emerging opportunities, and to keep supporting the businesses that drive our province's growth.

It is an administrative change. It will matter to the operation of that committee. I encourage all members to support it. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Let me be straight with the House. I am not a veterinarian, and I have never had to call one out at two in the morning for a calving gone wrong. So I have done a lot of listening on this file. This approach allows public resources to be refocused on their core mission while leveraging the expertise of the private sector for the delivery of routine care. We are not withdrawing. The goal is a more modern and sustainable model, aligned with Canadian best practices, so that veterinary services stay robust and are adapted to current and future challenges. The modernization will enable New Brunswick to build a model that can meet the specific needs of farms while guaranteeing high-quality services. I will admit that we did not get ahead of the concerns the implementation has caused. For remote regions there are real challenges concerning the quality and the cost of services, and in several of those regions access was already a considerable challenge before any of this began. A producer in Kent County told me last month that he waited eleven hours. That is why a support program for private sector veterinarians is being developed. One of its objectives is to help offset certain costs, like travel expenses, so that producers from all regions can continue to get the services they need. The responses that have been provided do not mean all the worries have been cleared up. I don't think they have. But they underscore our commitment to finding concrete solutions tailored to each situation. Laboratory services are a key part of the transition. They do the early detection of emerging diseases, they prevent health crises, and they underpin food safety, and the existing laboratories will remain fully operational throughout, so that no farmer's or veterinarian's work is disrupted. We still need consensus around what we are proposing, and its success will depend in large part on cooperation and on people choosing to take part with an open mind. I am still open to hearing your opinions, your ideas, and your worries. I have already changed my mind on one part of this.

I want to start by recognizing that this bill brings forward some long-overdue clarifications. It updates outdated language, replacing legal Latin with plain English. That might seem minor, but clarity matters. It also simplifies the processes for brewers and distillers to sell their products at approved farmers' markets, something small producers in New Brunswick have been asking for. A microbrewery or a craft distillery that can sell straight to customers at the Saint Andrews farmers' market, the St. George market, or the market in St. Stephen — the St. George one runs Saturday mornings — helps drive tourism, encourages entrepreneurship, and strengthens local economies. I applaud that part of the bill, Madam Speaker. It recognizes a sector that has truly taken off here in New Brunswick.

That said, modernization should never come without scrutiny. The caps are in the bill's own text: 500 000 L for brewers, 75 000 L for distillers, and that is when they are operating as agents under the New Brunswick Liquor Corporation. Put the two side by side. The brewers' ceiling is somewhere between six and a half and seven times the distillers'. And neither figure is set against anything — not against the agency limit that applies today, not against what the average craft producer in this province actually put out last year. The Corporation has those production numbers. This House does not.

So those sound like fair limits right up until you ask who they fit. Were these caps determined in consultation with our smaller producers, or primarily with larger operators? Will this inadvertently favour those already established in the market, making it harder for start-ups to grow into the next tier? We've seen well-intentioned changes to regulation end up benefitting those with deeper pockets and more connections, while small business owners struggle with compliance costs and licencing delays.

Craft producers in St. Croix, people who pour their life savings into starting a brewery or a distillery, say: We don't mind rules, but we just want fair ones. This is my question for the government: How will fairness between small and large producers be ensured under this new licencing model?

Mr. Speaker, today I want to congratulate two remarkable authors, Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck of L'nui Menikuk, also known as Indian Island First Nation, on their recent cookbook, Mitji— Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. It is a testament to the rich heritage and the resilient spirit of the people of Mi'gma'gi. This is not just a cookbook, Mr. Speaker. The recipes carry the historical knowledge and the lived experience of a community that has thrived on these lands for generations, and the authors do not stop at the food — they address the profound impacts of gastrocolonialism, which is to say how colonial policies altered traditional Indigenous recipes. That took work. Mr. Speaker, I invite all members to join me in congratulating Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck for their commitment to preserving Indigenous culinary traditions.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. The bill on long-term illness and injury leave protects workers, and it is an essential step forward. A person who gets sick should not have to pick between getting better and paying the mortgage. Again, Madam Speaker, this is not an ordinary bill. It is a concrete commitment to our people. A worker can take up to 27 weeks of protected leave and come back to the same position or an equivalent job. That means the employer holds the spot, the family keeps the paycheque coming as best it can, and nobody comes back to find their name off the schedule. The bill updates our employment standards so they match how people actually live: a diagnosis, a treatment schedule, a spouse doing the driving, a kid who still has to get to school. Madam Speaker, we bring in legislation like this to stand behind people when they are sick, when they are hurting, and when they are being treated unfairly. These are not housekeeping measures.

Madam Speaker, I rise today with great satisfaction and deep gratitude. After years of waiting, the new, hoped-for bridge between Île Lamèque and Shippagan will be built. I thank the Premier, Hon. Susan Holt, and the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure, Hon. Chuck Chiasson, for coming to the region in February and making that announcement, which marks a turning point for our communities. The bridge will simplify travel, strengthen our connections with the rest of the province, and bring new economic opportunities to our people. On behalf of my constituents, I want to express our gratitude to everyone who played a role in making this important project for our community happen. There was a man at the announcement in February with a photo of the old bridge in his coat pocket. He'd been carrying it around for years. He didn't say anything. He just showed it to me. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Well, I should say at the start that I am not an epidemiologist and I have not read every line of the Public Health Act. I have read the parts my staff flagged for me. That is honest.

But I lived through the same three years everybody in this Chamber did, and I saw what the pandemic did to our communities, our families, and our economy. So I am proposing a resolution calling on the government to take immediate action, before the next one.

Here is what I do understand. The Act is the cornerstone of the province's response and it is badly out of date. It says nothing about RSV. There is no mechanism in it for Public Health to add an illness to the ones it tracks — I asked about that in November and the letter I got back did not answer the question.

Now, readiness costs money: public health infrastructure, resources, personnel. I don't know what the number is. I know we did not have enough nurses in 2020 and I know we have fewer now.

And the response has to reach the people it missed. Seniors, people with underlying conditions, marginalized communities — they were hit hardest, and a strategy has to be built for their circumstances or it is not a strategy. My own mother waited nine days for a result in Fredericton, and she has a family doctor. Think about somebody who doesn't.

We should also be running education and awareness campaigns now, while nobody is frightened, because that is when people actually listen.

I ask all members to support the resolution.
